items.title: The Domesday Book recorded almost every pig in England
items.claim: William I commissioned the Domesday survey in 1085, completed 1086. How detailed was it?

options.text: It listed only the major landholders and royal manors
It recorded landholders, ploughs, mills, fishponds, livestock and even individual peasants down to the level of swineherds — over 13,000 places
It was a list of military obligations only

items.reveal_title: Not one ox or cow escaped
items.reveal:
The Anglo-Saxon Chronicle (E text) complained: 'So very narrowly did he have it investigated that there was no single hide nor a yard of land, nor indeed (it is a shame to relate but it seemed no shame to him to do) one ox nor one cow nor one pig which was left out.'

Commissioners visited every shire, took sworn testimony, and produced the survey in around a year. The original manuscripts (Great Domesday and Little Domesday) survive at The National Archives, Kew.
items.why: Medieval government is often dismissed as primitive. Domesday is more administratively detailed than anything attempted in Europe for centuries afterwards.

items.title: Medieval Europeans knew the Earth was round
items.claim: The idea that 'medieval people thought the Earth was flat' was popularised in the 19th century. Who is most responsible for spreading it?

options.text: Galileo, in his trial defence of 1633
Washington Irving's 1828 biography of Columbus, which fabricated a debate at Salamanca about whether Columbus would sail off the edge
Karl Marx, as part of his critique of religion

items.reveal:
Bede (8th century), Aquinas (13th century), Dante (14th century) and the entire scholastic tradition assumed a spherical Earth — it was Aristotelian orthodoxy reinforced by Ptolemy. Columbus's argument with the Salamanca scholars was about the Earth's circumference, not its shape; they thought (correctly) it was too large to sail to Asia westward.

Washington Irving's 'A History of the Life and Voyages of Christopher Columbus' (1828) was a partly fictionalised popular biography. It invented the flat-Earth debate to make Columbus look more visionary. The myth then became a stock anti-medieval, anti-Catholic talking point in the late 19th century (notably John William Draper and Andrew Dickson White).
items.why: Historiography matters. The 'Dark Ages' frame and the flat-Earth myth are products of later polemic, not medieval thought. The conflict-between-science-and-religion narrative is largely a 19th-century construction.

items.title: Harold won the first battle of 1066 — then lost the second three weeks later
items.claim: King Harold Godwinson fought two major battles in 1066. What happened?

options.text: Hastings was his only battle of the year
He defeated Harald Hardrada and Tostig at Stamford Bridge on 25 September, then marched 250 miles south and lost to William at Hastings on 14 October
He won at Hastings but died of wounds soon after
He defeated William at Hastings, then was killed by Harald Hardrada

items.reveal:
Harald Hardrada of Norway and Harold's exiled brother Tostig landed in Yorkshire in September 1066. Harold marched north and crushed them at Stamford Bridge on 25 September — Hardrada and Tostig were killed.

Three days later William of Normandy landed at Pevensey. Harold's exhausted army marched south and met William at Senlac Hill near Hastings on 14 October. The Anglo-Saxon Chronicle records Harold's death; the Bayeux Tapestry depicts a figure with an arrow to the eye, though the identification is debated.
items.why: The Conquest is taught as a single event. It was actually a year of crisis with two invasions, one of which Harold won. Without Stamford Bridge weakening his army, Hastings might have gone the other way.
